title: Decide what starts a workflow
description: Distinguish automatic and manual activation, recording scope and future cross-recording ideas.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional operator who wants routine processing on one camera and a deeper review only when investigating a case. Are those two different workflow systems?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Automatic and manual triggers feed the same engine and stages. Automatic triggers match arriving classified recordings. Manual triggers launch work for media the user selects from an enabled surface. One workflow can support both modes.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So the trigger explains why the work starts, not a different result format?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. Keep activation separate from what the stages do once a run begins.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does the operator avoid starting that routine workflow for every camera?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use the documented device and envelope conditions, together with the weekly schedule. Conditions combine, so each required predicate must hold. An empty condition list stays eligible broadly; it isn't a selection of zero cameras.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And schedules need more care than just saying overnight?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes. Review weekdays, time segments and timezone using the guide's conventions. Then test recordings inside and outside the intended window. A meaningful workflow name doesn't constrain the trigger.

chapters.title: Manual selection still creates recording-sized runs

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: If our operator selects three case recordings and presses Run, does that become one giant input video?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. The manual action fans out one run per selected recording. Each reports its own progress and results. The case provides the selection context, not an automatic merge of the clips.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The page also discusses reasoning across neighbouring recordings. Can we rely on that now?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Not on the forward-looking aggregation design. The guide marks that layer as unbuilt. Base today's integration on the implemented recording-sized runs, and verify both activation and returned results before expanding its scope.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
